Recorded context: terminal_speed_m_s=0.6351726092425104 (handle f81b1dbe1d67b) still exceeds the settling speed limit; late_max_error_m=0.05813810428573256 (handle ff47840769a24) and late_max_speed_m_s=1.5810152739742807 (handle f141a00f08e6f) are the recorded late-window extremes; deadline_misses=35 (handle f3e59cefcd307) with mean_update_s=17.075238151415917 s (handle f5e0c39558a9c) against control_period_s=0.01 s (handle fd49845c3b95b), stopping_counts User_Requested_Stop=34 (handle f43420decaa95) and Solve_Succeeded=1 (handle f569f5a2f1f35), configured horizon=10 (handle f775debbc81c6), and prediction-dominated weighting (tracking_weight=1.0 vs velocity_weight/terminal_velocity_weight=0.0001, terminal_weight=5.0, holding_tip_speed_weight=0.0 and terminal_tip_speed_weight=0.0). Which competing mechanisms best explain the failed settling: slow terminal approach not being braked within the short window (e.g. weak tip-speed/braking weighting relative to position tracking), per-update plan selection / selected-iteration and effective-horizon behavior across the 35 updates, repeated deadline misses inflating update latency, or residual backend-model mismatch between the one-step prediction and the measured backend motion? I ask for a bounded comparison of these candidates, not a dominant-cause verdict.
scope: Retained-evidence reads (no solve, no evaluation): source.summary already handed over; may read source.backend_motion via the derived motion view over sample_times_s [0.01, 0.35] focusing on the final settling window, and the endpoint_query view over selected controller updates (at most 8 update_ids per query) for measured backend position/velocity at matched next timestamps.
